The Story of Anantmati

Bowing with devotion to the feet of the blessed Arhant, bestower of the bliss of liberation, I write the story of Anantmati, through whom the desireless quality of right faith was revealed.

In the world, the land of Anga is well known. At the time of our story, its chief city was Champapuri. Its king was Vasuvardhan, and his queen was Lakshmimati. She was virtuous, gifted, and of a gentle nature. They had a son named Priyadatt. Priyadatt held unwavering faith in the Jain dharma. His wife was Angavati, a woman of great piety and generosity. To Angavati was born a daughter named Anantmati. She was exceedingly beautiful and an ocean of virtues.

The Ashtahnika festival arrived. Priyadatt went to the monk Dharmakirti and took a vow of brahmacharya for eight days. In a playful mood, he also bestowed the same vow upon his beloved daughter. Sometimes, the playful words of a saintly person become a guide to the path of truth.

The effect on Anantmati was profound. When the time came for her marriage and preparations were being made, Anantmati approached her father and said, "Father, did you not give me the vow of brahmacharya? Why then are you making these wedding arrangements?"

Priyadatt replied, "My dear daughter, the vow I gave you was merely in jest. Do you really take it as truth?"

Anantmati answered, "Father, how can there be jest in matters of dharma and vows? This I do not understand."

Priyadatt pressed further, "My dear child, the light of our family, I gave you that vow only playfully. But even if you take it seriously, it was only for eight days. Why then do you refuse to marry?"

Anantmati said, "I accept that in your mind you may have intended it for only eight days. But neither you nor the revered monk told me so at the time. How then could I know it was temporary? Therefore, whatever may come, I shall observe it for my entire life. I shall not marry."

Her father was deeply disappointed, but what could he do? He was compelled to abandon all his wedding plans. After this, he arranged for Anantmati to receive instruction from the monk Dharmakirti. She studied the scriptures diligently and, in time, asked for permission to take formal initiation as a Jain nun.

Her parents, though heartbroken at the thought of parting with their beloved daughter, could see that her resolve was unshakeable. With tears in their eyes and blessings on their lips, they gave their consent. Anantmati took the vows of a Jain nun under the guidance of Dharmakirti.

As a nun, Anantmati observed every vow with meticulous care. She practised non-violence in thought, word, and deed. She studied the sacred texts with deep understanding. She bore every hardship — hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and the harsh words of others — with serene equanimity. She spent her days in meditation, study, and service to her fellow nuns.

Her conduct was so pure and her understanding so deep that she became a teacher and guide to many. Women from far and wide came to learn from her, and her influence spread throughout the Jain community. She taught that the soul, in its true nature, is free from all desire, and that liberation comes only when every craving — even the subtlest — is extinguished.

Through years of dedicated practice, Anantmati destroyed all her karmic bonds. At the end of her life, she attained moksha — the eternal state of infinite knowledge, infinite perception, infinite bliss, and infinite energy.

The story of Anantmati teaches us that a vow, once taken, must be honoured regardless of the intention behind it. The power of a vow lies not in the mind of the giver but in the sincerity of the one who keeps it. Anantmati showed that even a casual word, received with a pure heart, can become the turning point of an entire life. And she proved that desirelessness — the complete absence of longing for worldly life — is the truest mark of right faith.
